Title: The Ramayana of Valmiki (critical edition translation)
Creator: Valmiki (attrib.); tr. Robert P. Goldman, Sally J. Sutherland Goldman and others
Year: c. 5th c. BCE to 3rd c. CE; tr. 1984 to 2017; one volume 2021
Central women characters: Sita, Kaikeyi, Kaushalya, Surpanakha, Mandodari, Tara, Ahalya, Shabari, Manthara, Trijata
Distinctive characterisation: The base the retellings answer. Sita insists on going to the forest and taunts Rama as "a woman with a man's form" when he hesitates; she rebukes him before the fire; in the Uttara Kanda she refuses a second test and returns to the earth.
Why it matters: You need it to show what each retelling keeps, cuts or overturns; read the Ayodhya, Sundara, Yuddha (fire) and Uttara sections first.
Reviews and responses: See Sutherland Goldman, "The Voice of Sita in Valmiki's Sundarakanda" (2001) in this corpus
English translation: Yes: Princeton critical edition translation, 7 vols; one volume 2021 (ISBN 9780691206868)

Title: Dasaratha Jataka
Creator: Pali Buddhist Jataka (anonymous)
Distinctive characterisation: Rama, Lakkhana and Sita are siblings; Sita becomes Rama's queen after the exile; no abduction, no war and no fire test.
Why it matters: Ambedkar cites it; it unsettles both the idea of one original story and the marriage plot itself.

Title: Ramopakhyana (the Rama episode of the Mahabharata)
Creator: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (anonymous)
Distinctive characterisation: A short telling that ends with the return and coronation: there is no banishment of Sita.
Why it matters: Shows the abandonment of Sita is not in every early telling; useful when you argue the exile is a later choice.

Title: Paumacariya (Jain Ramayana)
Creator: Vimalasuri
Distinctive characterisation: After the ordeal Sita takes diksha and becomes a Jain nun, and other women follow her; Kaikeyi does not demand the exile; Ravana is a just king with one weakness.
Why it matters: Renunciation as Sita's own exit: a non-Hindu telling where she chooses her ending.
Reviews and responses: K.R. Chandra, A Critical Study of Paumacariyam (1970); V.M. Kulkarni, The Story of Rama in Jain Literature; LiveHistoryIndia feature
Check note: Dating varies widely by source.

Title: Raghuvamsha, canto 14 (Sita's message)
Creator: Kalidasa
Distinctive characterisation: The abandoned, pregnant Sita sends Rama a message through Lakshmana: restrained and dignified, but pointed, asking whether this act suits his line.
Why it matters: An early classical model of the restrained rebuke: voice without revolt, useful for Hypothesis B.

Title: Padmacarita
Creator: Ravisena
Distinctive characterisation: A Sanskrit Jain telling that keeps Sita's turn to renunciation after the ordeal.
Why it matters: Shows the Jain ending lived on in Sanskrit, not only in Prakrit.

Title: Uttararamacarita
Creator: Bhavabhuti
Distinctive characterisation: Rama's grief is centre stage; in Act 3 an unseen Sita watches him mourn while the forest goddess Vasanti reproaches him; the play ends in reunion, not in the earth.
Why it matters: Compassion for Sita without giving her the last word; read with Shulman's essay on its "cruelty and compassion".
Reviews and responses: David Shulman, "Bhavabhuti on Cruelty and Compassion", in Questioning Ramayanas (2001)

Title: Iramavataram (Kamba Ramayanam)
Creator: Kamban
Distinctive characterisation: Rama and Sita fall in love at first sight before the bow test; Surpanakha's approach is expanded; the fire test is staged with great feeling; Ahalya is less guilty than in Valmiki.
Why it matters: Key Tamil source for Erndl's Surpanakha comparison and for "Fire and Flood".

Title: Adbhuta Ramayana
Creator: Anonymous (attributed to Valmiki)
Distinctive characterisation: When Rama falls before the thousand-headed Ravana, Sita takes the form of Kali and kills him; Sita is born of Mandodari; the text contains a Sita Sahasranama.
Why it matters: The classical warrant for a "warrior Sita", cited in the 2026 film debate.
Reviews and responses: Ruth Vanita, "The Sita Who Smiles" (Manushi 148, 2005)

Title: Adhyatma Ramayana
Creator: Anonymous (part of the Brahmanda Purana)
Distinctive characterisation: Introduces the shadow Sita: the real Sita waits in the fire while an illusory Sita is abducted, so the fire test simply swaps them back.
Why it matters: The shadow device protects her purity by erasing her experience; central to Hypothesis B and to Tulsidas.

Title: Krittivasi Ramayan
Creator: Krittibas Ojha
Distinctive characterisation: The most popular Bengali Ramayana: devotional and full of local colour; Stewart and Dimock read a quiet critique of Rama's kingship in it.
Why it matters: The Bengali mainstream against which Chandrabati and Dev Sen are read.
Reviews and responses: Tony K. Stewart and Edward C. Dimock, "Krttibasa's Apophatic Critique of Rama's Kingship", in Questioning Ramayanas (2001)

Title: Bilanka Ramayana
Creator: Sarala Das (attrib.)
Distinctive characterisation: Sita takes the form of Kali to kill the thousand-headed Ravana of Patala (Bilanka).
Why it matters: An Odia parallel to the Adbhuta: the fierce Sita was not marginal.

Title: Ananda Ramayana
Creator: Anonymous
Distinctive characterisation: A Vaishnava telling that adds many new episodes and rituals; Aklujkar studies its humour.
Why it matters: Kalakshetra drew verses from it; shows expansion rather than critique.
Reviews and responses: Vidyut Aklujkar, "Crying Dogs and Laughing Trees", in Questioning Ramayanas (2001)
Check note: Dating approximate.

Title: Molla Ramayanam
Creator: Atukuri Molla
Distinctive characterisation: A devout telling in plain Telugu, in six kandas, by a woman from a potter (Kummara) family; it follows Valmiki closely and does not criticise Rama.
Why it matters: Authorship is the intervention: Dev Sen contrasts Molla (male eyes) with Chandrabati (women's eyes). Tests Hypothesis C on who counts as feminist.
Reviews and responses: Nabaneeta Dev Sen, "Rewriting the Ramayana: Chandrabati and Molla"

Title: Chandrabati's Ramayan
Creator: Chandrabati
Distinctive characterisation: Opens with Mandodari and Sita's birth and gives the story to Sita; the war is compressed; Sita's twelve-month lament (baromasi) carries the narrative; Rama's sister Kukua tricks Sita into drawing Ravana, which brings her banishment.
Why it matters: Your anchor for Field I and Hypothesis D: a woman's telling, for women listeners, that judges Rama.
Reviews and responses: Parabaas (Nandini Gupta); Open Letters Review; Sanglap 11.1 (Priti Mandal, Dec 2024); Purple Pencil Project
Author contact: Poet 16th c.; translator Dev Sen died 2019; publisher Zubaan
English translation: Yes: Dev Sen, Zubaan 2020 (ISBN 9789385932946); also Bose and Bose, Routledge 2013
Told through: Sita, from her birth; the poet speaks to women listeners

Title: Ramcharitmanas
Creator: Tulsidas
Distinctive characterisation: Sita as the ideal devoted wife; the shadow Sita; Rama's harsh words at the fire are cut; Shabari's devotion is honoured; the Sundarkand line "dhol, ganvar, shudra, pashu, nari" remains a flashpoint.
Why it matters: The text most Hindi speakers know; the reference point for Hess, Kishwar, Anamika and Hindi women's songs.
Reviews and responses: Linda Hess, "Lovers' Doubts: Questioning the Tulsi Ramayan" (2001); Pauwels 2008

Title: The Ramayana of Hamida Banu Begum, Queen Mother of Mughal India
Creator: Manuscript owned by Hamida Banu Begum; study by John Seyller, Marika Sardar and Audrey Truschke
Distinctive characterisation: A Persian translation of the Ramayana with 56 paintings, owned by Akbar's mother.
Why it matters: A woman reader and patron of the Ramayana inside a Muslim court: widens Field I beyond women authors.
Author contact: Audrey Truschke (Rutgers): faculty page via search (search link)
English translation: Yes (book, Museum of Islamic Art Doha / Silvana 2020)

Title: Hikayat Seri Rama
Creator: Anonymous
Distinctive characterisation: Ravana (Maharaja Wana) is more sympathetic than an arrogant Rama; the story lives inside Islamic court culture; the oldest manuscript is in the Bodleian (Laud, 1635).
Why it matters: A Muslim, Southeast Asian telling that moves sympathy around; useful for religion (Field VII).
Reviews and responses: British Library Asian and African Studies blog (2014)

Title: Ramchandrika
Creator: Keshavdas
Distinctive characterisation: A courtly Braj Ramayana that shows off metres and figures of speech; Sita appears through the conventions of riti poetry.
Why it matters: A Braj text you can read in the original: a contrast between the courtly Sita and the Sita of women's songs.
Check note: Pick an edition before reading.

Title: Dastan-i Ram u Sita (Ramayan-i Masihi)
Creator: Masih Panipati
Distinctive characterisation: A Persian masnavi of about 5,300 verses, dedicated to Jahangir, that makes the epic a love story; women such as Kaikeyi and Ravana's sister get more narrative space.
Why it matters: Persian is one of your languages: a direct route into Indo-Persian Ramayanas (about 51 Persian versions exist).
Reviews and responses: Audrey Truschke excerpt in Scroll; Iranian study comparing women in Masih and Valmiki

Title: Ramayanasara (Sanskrit rendering of the king's Telugu Ramayana)
Creator: Madhuravani
Year: 17th c. (court of Raghunatha Nayak, r. 1600 to 1634)
Distinctive characterisation: A court poetess renders the king's Telugu Ramayana into Sanskrit in 14 cantos.
Why it matters: A woman inside the courtly canon: complicates the easy divide of folk = women and classical = men.
Reviews and responses: "Madhuravani, the Sanskrit Poetess of Tanjore", Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society

Title: Vashista Ramayanam
Creator: Tarigonda Vengamamba
Distinctive characterisation: A devotional Telugu telling in dwipada couplets by a poet who refused the marks of widowhood.
Why it matters: Devotional authorship backed by a defiant life; widowhood links to Field V (body).
Check note: Text content not yet checked.

Title: Ramakien
Creator: Court of King Rama I (version)
Distinctive characterisation: A demoness tricks Sita into drawing Ravana's portrait; it is placed under Rama's bed and leads to her banishment.
Why it matters: The portrait motif also appears in Chandrabati (through Kukua): a travelling women's-story element.

Title: Sita Swayamvar
Creator: Vishnudas Bhave
Distinctive characterisation: Usually counted as the first modern Marathi play: a Ramayana wedding story put on stage.
Why it matters: The start of the Ramayana on the Marathi stage, the line Warerkar later breaks.

Title: Persian Ramayana of Mohar Singh
Creator: Mohar Singh
Distinctive characterisation: Sita prays that the fire become a rose garden, as it did for Ibrahim; Trijata compares Rama to Isa (Jesus).
Why it matters: Islamic and Christian images inside Sita's ordeal: a striking case for Field VII.
Reviews and responses: Pritam Saini, The Tribune (2002)
Check note: Exact date not confirmed.

Title: Sitar Banabas (The Exile of Sita)
Creator: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
Distinctive characterisation: A reformer's prose retelling of Sita's exile, drawn from Bhavabhuti, for a new Bengali reading public.
Why it matters: Links Sita's exile to the 19th-century reform debates on women and to early Bengali prose.
Check note: A prose narrative (listed under Novel); check edition.
Told through: A narrator who dwells on Sita's grief in exile

Title: Meghnadbadh Kavya (The Slaying of Meghanada)
Creator: Michael Madhusudan Dutt
Distinctive characterisation: Sympathy shifts to Lanka; Meghnad's wife Pramila leads a band of women warriors to reach her husband and later dies on his pyre; Sita tells her story to the rakshasi Sarama.
Why it matters: A colonial epic told from Ravana's side; Pramila's martial courage ending in sati complicates agency (Hypothesis B).
Reviews and responses: Clinton Seely, "The Raja's New Clothes: Redressing Ravana in Meghanadavadha Kavya", in Many Ramayanas (1991)
English translation: Yes: The Slaying of Meghanada: A Ramayana from Colonial Bengal (OUP 2004)

Title: "Sita" (in Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan)
Creator: Toru Dutt
Distinctive characterisation: Three children listen as their mother tells of Sita's second exile, and all of them weep: the story lives in the home.
Why it matters: A colonial woman poet writing in English places Sita inside domestic storytelling (Hypothesis A).

Title: Kabye Upekshita (The Neglected Women of Poetry)
Creator: Rabindranath Tagore
Distinctive characterisation: Tagore names Urmila as the heroine the poets forgot.
Why it matters: The start of the "neglected Urmila" line that runs through Dwivedi, Saket and Kane's Sita's Sister.
Check note: Year: check (given as 1900 to 1907).

Title: Kaviyon ki Urmila Vishayak Udasinta (The Poets' Neglect of Urmila)
Creator: Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi
Distinctive characterisation: The editor of Saraswati urges Hindi poets to write about Urmila.
Why it matters: The bridge from Tagore to Gupt's Saket in Hindi.
Check note: Title wording and year: check.

Title: Ramayan ka ek Scene (A Scene from the Ramayana)
Creator: Brij Narayan Chakbast
Distinctive characterisation: Rama takes leave of his mother Kaushalya: a mother's grief in the Urdu elegiac style of soz and marsiya.
Why it matters: A mother's sorrow at the centre (Hypothesis A) and the shared Hindu and Muslim world of Urdu poetry (Field VII).
Check note: Year: check.

Title: Lanka Dahan (film)
Creator: Dadasaheb Phalke (dir.); Anna Salunke as Rama and Sita
Distinctive characterisation: A male actor, Anna Salunke, plays both Rama and Sita.
Why it matters: Gender on screen begins with cross-casting: a starting point for Field VI.

Title: Chintavishtayaya Sita (Sita Immersed in Thought)
Creator: Kumaran Asan
Distinctive characterisation: Alone after sending her sons to Rama's court, Sita looks back on her life, judges Rama's choices and moves towards her end with self-respect.
Why it matters: A landmark of Sita's inner voice in 1919, long before "feminist retellings".
Translator: Rizio Yohannan Raj ("The Pensive Queen", in Richman 2008)
English translation: Yes (Richman 2008; also "Sita: Her Untold Story", Authorspress 2017)
Told through: Sita, alone, judging her life and Rama's choices

Title: Sita Agnipravesam (Sita Enters the Fire)
Creator: Gudipati Venkata Chalam
Distinctive characterisation: Sita is a rebel and a logical thinker: she says Ravana was nobler than Rama because he asked for her love and did not treat her as a machine for heirs, and she walks into Ravana's pyre.
Why it matters: A radical, male-authored "feminist" Sita: voice can come from male reformers too (Hypothesis C).
Translator: Sailaza Easwari Pal ("Talking Back: Sita Enters the Fire", in Richman 2008)
Check note: Year 1924 as given by Volga (Scroll, 2017).

Title: Panchavati
Creator: Maithili Sharan Gupt
Distinctive characterisation: A long poem on the Panchavati episode, including Surpanakha's approach to Lakshmana.
Why it matters: Read with Erndl's "Mutilation of Surpanakha", which includes modern Hindi verse.

Title: Saket
Creator: Maithili Sharan Gupt
Distinctive characterisation: Urmila's separation fills the epic; in Canto 8 Kaikeyi repents in public at Chitrakoot; the tone is nationalist and devotional.
Why it matters: The Hindi Urmila classic. Shanta Gokhale argues it gave Urmila no real substance or voice: test Hypothesis B here.
Reviews and responses: Shanta Gokhale column (2015) on Saket and Urmila
English translation: Partial; a full English transcreation by Anand Kumar Ashodhiya (ISBN 9789354698453; year: check)
Told through: Urmila, waiting in Ayodhya; Kaikeyi repents

Title: Seeta (film)
Creator: Debaki Bose (dir.); Durga Khote as Sita, Prithviraj Kapoor as Rama
Distinctive characterisation: A film of the Uttara Kanda and Sita's exile; the first Indian talkie shown at an international festival (Venice, 1934).
Why it matters: Early cinema chooses Sita's suffering as its subject.

Title: Ram Rajya (film)
Creator: Vijay Bhatt (dir.); Shobhana Samarth as Sita
Distinctive characterisation: Shobhana Samarth's Sita became the calendar image of the ideal wife; often said to be the only film Gandhi watched.
Why it matters: How the nationalist ideal Sita was made: a contrast case.

Title: Saapa Vimochanam (Deliverance from the Curse)
Creator: Pudumaippittan
Distinctive characterisation: Ahalya, freed from stone, meets Sita and learns of the fire ordeal; she chooses to turn back into stone.
Why it matters: One woman reads another's ordeal and refuses the world: a sharp case against liberation by voice alone (Hypothesis B).

Title: Shudra Tapasvi
Creator: Kuvempu
Distinctive characterisation: Rama is made to see the injustice of killing the Shudra ascetic Shambuka.
Why it matters: The caste side of the Uttara Kanda, whose two victims are a woman and a Shudra (Field IV).
Check note: Year: check.

Title: Sri Ramayana Darshanam
Creator: Kuvempu
Distinctive characterisation: At the fire ordeal Rama rushes into the flames after Sita and walks out holding her hand.
Why it matters: A canonical, award-winning epic that shares the ordeal between husband and wife instead of cancelling it.
Reviews and responses: Sahitya Akademi Award; Jnanpith Award (1967)

Title: Bhoomikanya Sita
Creator: Mama (B.V.) Warerkar
Distinctive characterisation: Urmila is central and protests the ordeals; Sita returns to the earth; the myth is read through the tiller of the land. Natya Niketan refused to stage it.
Why it matters: Ties Sita to land and labour (Fields IV and V) and gives Urmila a political voice.
Reviews and responses: Shanta Gokhale column, 11 Mar 2015
Check note: Publication year conflict: 1955 (Gokhale) vs 1958. A Sanskrit translation, Bhumikanya, by Ratnamayi Devi Dikshit (1967 to 1968) is reported in one source: check.

Title: Ramkatha: Utpatti aur Vikas (The Rama Story: Origins and Growth)
Creator: Camille Bulcke
Distinctive characterisation: A vast survey of Rama stories across languages and religions, tracing how episodes such as Sita's birth and exile changed.
Why it matters: A Hindi classic you can read in the original: a map of variants for every chapter.
English translation: Yes: The Rama Story: Origins and Growth (Sahitya Akademi)

Title: Asokavanam
Creator: Kodavatiganti Kutumba Rao
Distinctive characterisation: A Telugu story set in the Asoka grove, cited by Volga as part of the rationalist rewriting line in Telugu.
Why it matters: Context for Volga's own lineage.
Check note: Content not checked; cited by Volga.

Title: The Riddle of Rama and Krishna (Riddles in Hinduism, Appendix I)
Creator: B.R. Ambedkar
Distinctive characterisation: Attacks Rama's treatment of Sita (the fire test, the banishment, her refusal of a second test) and of Vali; cites the Buddhist Jataka where Sita is Rama's sister.
Why it matters: The anti-caste critique of Rama as husband and king; its 1987 publication caused a political storm (Field VII).
Reviews and responses: Full text: Writings and Speeches vol. 4 (Govt of Maharashtra, 1987)

Title: Ramayana Patirangal / The Ramayana: A True Reading (Hindi: Sachchi Ramayan)
Creator: E.V. Ramasamy (Periyar); Hindi edition published by Lalai Singh Yadav
Distinctive characterisation: Reads the Ramayana as Aryan conquest of the Dravidian south: Ravana is the wronged hero and Rama the aggressor; Sita is treated harshly as part of the attack on Rama.
Why it matters: The anti-caste reversal of heroes, which does not by itself free Sita (Hypothesis C). The Supreme Court upheld the Hindi edition in 1976.
Reviews and responses: Supreme Court judgment, 16 Sep 1976; Forward Press Hindi edition 2020 (intro V. Geetha)
Author contact: Not applicable (d. 1973); Hindi edition: Forward Press

Title: Kanchana Sita (play)
Creator: C.N. Sreekantan Nair
Distinctive characterisation: Sita is absent in body and present as nature, while Rama is tested by his own idea of dharma.
Why it matters: Basis of Aravindan's film; Kendra Sahitya Akademi Award 1962.
Reviews and responses: Vinod C. Khanna, The Book Review 30(1), Jan 2006
English translation: Yes (Retelling the Ramayana: Voices from Kerala, OUP 2005)

Title: Kathanayika Molla (film)
Creator: B. Padmanabham (dir.)
Distinctive characterisation: A popular film on the life of the poet Molla.
Why it matters: Shows how a woman poet's life was turned into cinema.

Title: Seetha Josyam
Creator: Narla Venkateswara Rao
Distinctive characterisation: Sita openly criticises Rama's campaigns against the forest peoples, waged on behalf of the ascetics.
Why it matters: Sita as a political critic of conquest (Field IV).
Check note: Year not confirmed. Sort year is an estimate for the timeline.

Title: When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision
Creator: Adrienne Rich
Distinctive characterisation: Defines re-vision as "entering an old text from a new critical direction" as an act of survival for women.
Why it matters: The root of your concept "revisionist mythmaking".

Title: Ramayana painting (1974) and Mithila Sita imagery
Creator: Sita Devi (c. 1912 to 2005)
Distinctive characterisation: A leading Mithila painter, Padma Shri 1981, renders the Ramayana in the women's wall-painting tradition of the region where Sita is a daughter.
Why it matters: Women's visual authorship: Field VI and Hypothesis D through images, not words.

Title: Ramayana Vishavruksham (Ramayana the Poisonous Tree)
Creator: Ranganayakamma
Distinctive characterisation: A Marxist rereading built from Valmiki itself: 16 stories, linking essays and 504 footnotes expose class, caste and gender power in the "ideal" kingdom.
Why it matters: The most systematic Marxist feminist rewriting; a test of Structural feminism (Field IV).
Reviews and responses: Reprinted more often than Viswanatha's Ramayana Kalpavrukshamu (author's site)
Told through: The author, arguing with Valmiki's text (openly feminist and Marxist)

Title: Where Shall We Go This Summer?
Creator: Anita Desai
Distinctive characterisation: A pregnant, middle-aged woman named Sita leaves her Bombay home for the island of Manori, wishing not to give birth into a violent world.
Why it matters: A modern namesake: tests how much the name "Sita" carries (Fields II and V, motherhood).
Reviews and responses: Discussed in Sutapa Chaudhuri (2013)
Told through: Sita, a pregnant wife who leaves for an island

Title: Kanchana Sita (film)
Creator: G. Aravindan (dir.)
Distinctive characterisation: Sita never appears in human form: she is present as nature (Prakriti). Rama Chenchu tribal people play the heroes; Urmila asks whether man can be separate from nature.
Why it matters: The key film for Field V (ecofeminism) and for caste on screen (Field IV).
Reviews and responses: Ankita Menon (2025); Usha Zacharias in Richman 2008; MUBI Notebook

Title: Nietzsche, Genealogy, History (in Language, Counter-Memory, Practice)
Creator: Michel Foucault
Distinctive characterisation: Genealogy and counter-memory: history as many descents rather than one origin.
Why it matters: Your concept "counter-memory": frames women's songs as memory against the official epic.

Title: The Ramayana Tradition in Asia
Creator: V. Raghavan (ed.)
Distinctive characterisation: Conference papers on Ramayanas across South and Southeast Asia.
Why it matters: Background for the Southeast Asian entries (Hikayat, Ramakien).

Title: The Thieves of Language: Women Poets and Revisionist Mythmaking
Creator: Alicia Ostriker
Distinctive characterisation: Women poets steal and remake old myths, turning familiar stories to their own ends.
Why it matters: Gives you the term "revisionist mythmaking" and a test for when it works.

Title: The Development of the Sita Myth: A Case Study of Women in Myth and Literature
Creator: Uma Chakravarti
Distinctive characterisation: Traces how Sita was shaped into the model of wifely devotion and how that model served patriarchy over time.
Why it matters: The historian's foundation for your project, by a scholar who taught at Miranda House.
Author contact: No public direct contact found; consider Miranda House and DU history networks (search link)

Title: "Shabari" (To Shabari)
Creator: Hira Bansode
Distinctive characterisation: A Dalit poet asks Shabari why she offered Rama berries instead of asking about Eklavya's thumb and Sita's exile.
Why it matters: The anti-caste feminist voice that the Sita-centred canon leaves out (Hypothesis C).
Reviews and responses: Saloni Walia, Setu (Oct 2018)
Check note: Year of the poem: check. Sort year is an estimate for the timeline.

Title: Ramayan (TV serial)
Creator: Ramanand Sagar (creator); Doordarshan
Distinctive characterisation: The Doordarshan serial that fixed a pan-Indian image of a calm, obedient Sita; Sunday mornings emptied the streets.
Why it matters: The reception baseline for Mankekar, Lutgendorf, Thapar and Rajagopal (Field VII).

Title: Sitayana: Epic of the Earth-born
Creator: K.R. Srinivasa Iyengar
Distinctive characterisation: An English epic of Sita's life as daughter of the earth.
Why it matters: Uses your project's title word: cite it when you define "Sitayan".
Check note: Publisher and year: check.
Told through: Sita as the earth-born

Title: Three Hundred Ramayanas: Five Examples and Three Thoughts on Translation
Creator: A.K. Ramanujan
Year: 1987 (talk); 1991 (in Many Ramayanas); removed from the DU syllabus 2011
Distinctive characterisation: Argues there is no single original Ramayana, only a common pool of tellings; compares episodes such as Ahalya's across languages.
Why it matters: Delhi University removed it from the BA History syllabus on 9 Oct 2011 after protests: a live case for Field VII at your own university.
Reviews and responses: Bharati Jaganathan, Mainstream (2011); Hartosh Singh Bal, Open (2011); SACW dossier

Title: Bargaining with Patriarchy
Creator: Deniz Kandiyoti
Distinctive characterisation: Women strategise within the limits of a given patriarchy; older women can gain power by enforcing its rules.
Why it matters: Explains Kaikeyi, Manthara and Kaushalya better than "victim or villain" (Field III).

Title: Can the Subaltern Speak?
Creator: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
Distinctive characterisation: Asks whether the subaltern woman can be heard when others speak for her; sati is the central case.
Why it matters: Your concept "subalternity": warns against assuming a retelling "gives voice".

Title: Staying Alive: Women, Ecology and Survival in India
Creator: Vandana Shiva
Distinctive characterisation: Links women, nature and the feminine principle (Prakriti) against Western development.
Why it matters: One side of the ecofeminism debate for Field V.

Title: Recasting Women: Essays in Colonial History
Creator: Kumkum Sangari and Sudesh Vaid (eds)
Distinctive characterisation: Essays on reform, nationalism and gender, including Partha Chatterjee's "The Nationalist Resolution of the Women's Question".
Why it matters: Explains why the 19th and 20th centuries needed an ideal Sita.

Title: Sita and Draupadi: Aggressive Behavior and Female Role-Models in the Sanskrit Epics
Creator: Sally J. Sutherland
Distinctive characterisation: Contrasts the passive, self-directed aggression of Sita with Draupadi's open anger as two models for women.
Why it matters: Gives you vocabulary for Sita's "turned inward" protest (Hypothesis B).

Title: The Perfect Wife: The Orthodox Hindu Woman according to the Stridharmapaddhati
Creator: Julia Leslie
Distinctive characterisation: Studies an 18th-century Sanskrit manual on the duties of wives.
Why it matters: The normative rulebook behind the "ideal Sita" (dharma question).

Title: The Ramayana Syndrome
Creator: Romila Thapar
Distinctive characterisation: Warns that the TV serial turned many Ramayanas into one official version.
Why it matters: The historian's warning that frames Field VII.

Title: Ramayan: The Video
Creator: Philip Lutgendorf
Distinctive characterisation: Studies the making and devotional viewing of Sagar's serial.
Why it matters: Core reception study for Field VII.

Title: Sita's Daughters (dance-theatre)
Creator: Mallika Sarabhai (with John Martin)
Distinctive characterisation: A performance about women who refuse patriarchy, staged more than 500 times; it drew right-wing backlash.
Why it matters: Performance as activism: Fields VI and VII together.

Title: A Ramayana of Their Own: Women's Oral Tradition in Telugu
Creator: Velcheru Narayana Rao
